portal.short: The Centre, what it runs, and the questions it is asked
portal.title: Computing Resources Centre
portal.lede: The network, your accounts, your email, the software you may install and the machines your research runs on — and, said plainly, the parts of that the university has not yet decided.
portal.description: The Computing Resources Centre's pages: getting on to the network from off campus, remote access to national computing, an introduction to Linux and SSH, software entitlement, and the computing questions the university has not yet answered.

notice.title: The Centre is a proposal, and most of these answers are missing
paragraphs: No unit of this name appears anywhere the university publishes, and no computing office appears in its directory of administrative offices. The name is a proposal; the service it describes is real work somebody does, and the pages here are what that work has to publish before anybody can use it.

So an answer here is one of three things: a fact read off a page the university published, with the address it was read from beside it; a question nobody has answered, kept and marked as such; or a sample, marked as a sample, showing the shape of an instruction the real version will replace. Nothing on these pages is a plausible guess, and that is the only guarantee they offer.

sections.title: What the Centre is answerable for
paragraphs: Everything a member of this university touches that is not paper. Six areas, and they are listed here rather than left implied because a service nobody has been made answerable for is a service that is nobody's to fix at four o'clock on a Friday.

items.label: The network
items.value: Wired and wireless on campus, the connection out to the internet, and — when it exists — the route back in from outside it.

items.label: Accounts and identity
items.value: One sign-in per person: when it starts working, what it opens, and what happens to it when the person leaves.

items.label: Email
items.value: The address, where it is read, and how long it lasts after graduation or resignation.

items.label: Software and licensing
items.value: What each kind of member may install, at whose cost, and what happens to the licence when they go.

items.label: Research computing
items.value: Machines larger than a workstation, whether the university's own or reached remotely at a national facility.

items.label: Security
items.value: Phishing, compromised accounts, what to do first, and who to tell.

sections.title: How to reach the Centre
paragraphs: It cannot be reached. Every field below is what a reader of this page would expect to find, and every one of them is empty, because the university publishes no telephone number, no email address, no room and no request system for computing.

That is the first thing on the work list at the foot of this page, and it is first because nothing else here can be acted on without it: a page that ends "ask the Computing Resources Centre" and cannot say how is a page that has answered nothing.

portal.questionsTitle: The questions the Centre is asked
questionsIntroduction: In the words people actually use, rather than in the names of the systems involved. Several have an answer already; the ones that do not are marked plainly rather than filled in with something plausible.
An unanswered question here is not an oversight. It is a decision the university has still to take and publish, and it is on the work list at the foot of this page so that somebody can take it.

topics.title: Joining, leaving and your accounts
topics.summary: What you are given on the day you arrive, and what happens to it on the day you go.

items.question: I have just joined. What accounts do I get, and when do they start working?
items.unanswered: Nobody has published what a new student or a new member of staff is given, on what day it becomes usable, or what to do if it has not by the time teaching starts. This is one of the two most-asked questions in any institution and one of the least often written down.

items.question: I have forgotten my password, or my account is locked
items.unanswered: No reset route, no self-service page and no identity check is published. Somebody has to decide how a person proves who they are before an account is unlocked, and where that happens.

items.question: I am leaving. What happens to my account, my email and my files?
items.unanswered: Nothing is published about how long an account survives, whether mail can be forwarded, what becomes of files held in university systems, or how much notice anyone gets. It is the question nobody asks until the day it is too late to ask it, and it has real consequences for research data.

facts.text: The university's offboarding is not described anywhere in what it publishes; its administrative offices index names Human Resources for employee matters and nobody for computing.

topics.title: Email
topics.summary: The address you are given and how long you keep it.

items.question: What is my university email address, and where do I read it?
items.unanswered: No page says that accounts are issued, in what form the address is made, which mail service holds it, or how to sign in to it. The university's own pages refer to a student's official email address as though everyone already has one.

facts.text: Several pages instruct students to use their official email id — for the student council and for examination correspondence — without anywhere saying how one is obtained.

items.question: Can I keep my university email address after I graduate?
items.unanswered: Not published. Alumni are offered library membership on payment and an alumni portal, so the university has taken a position on some post-graduation services and not on this one.

facts.text: Library membership is offered to alumni on a payment basis, which shows the question of continuing services after graduation has been considered elsewhere.

topics.title: Getting online, on campus and off
topics.summary: Wireless here, wireless elsewhere, and reaching university systems from home.

items.question: I cannot get on to the wireless network
items.unanswered: No network name, no joining instructions, no registration step and nobody to ask. What is published is only that the network exists and is meant to be always on.

facts.text: The campus amenities page says the university offers 24/7 WiFi facilities, and gives no further detail.
Hostel rooms are listed as having 24x7 Wi-Fi access.

The library provides PCs, LAN switches and Wi-Fi for personal laptops under a bring-your-own-device arrangement, which is the only place on the site where connecting a personal machine is described at all.

items.question: I am visiting another university. Can I use their wireless with my MIT-WPU sign-in?
items.unanswered: Eduroam is not mentioned anywhere the university publishes, so whether it is a member is unknown. It is worth answering in one line either way: a researcher who travels finds out at the worst moment.

items.question: A visitor is coming to see me. How do they get online?
items.unanswered: No guest access, sponsor process or visitor account is described. Anyone hosting an external examiner, a speaker or a conference has nothing to tell them.

items.question: I am at home and I cannot reach the library's journals and databases
answer: You are not meant to be able to. The library's electronic resources are licensed by network address and the university states that they work within its premises, so a subscription that opens on campus will refuse you at home.
There is no published remote access of any kind: no VPN, no proxy, no off-campus sign-in. Whether one exists is one of the questions at the foot of this page.
Before you write to anyone: the library also lists freely available national collections, which do work from anywhere.

facts.text: The Knowledge Resource Centre states that its online IP-based e-resources allow access anywhere on campus, and that its subscribed databases are accessible within the university premises.

links.label: Knowledge Resource Centre, including the free national collections

items.question: Can I reach my office machine, or a departmental server, from home?
items.unanswered: No remote-working provision of any kind is published. For a university that examines its students remotely, that is a conspicuous asymmetry: the students work off campus by design and the staff have nothing written down.

topics.title: Software, printing and where your work lives
topics.summary: What you may install, what you may print, and what happens to the file you were working on.

items.question: Is MATLAB — or Office, or Windows — free to me?
items.unanswered: No entitlement of any kind is published. Do not buy on the strength of a colleague's recollection and do not install on the strength of an assumption; the table further down this page is where the answer will go once somebody has it.

links.label: The software entitlement table, and what is still missing from it

items.question: I need a package installed on the machines in a teaching laboratory
items.unanswered: No route, no lead time and no approval step is published. Laboratories evidently do carry licensed software, so somebody is arranging it; nothing says who or how far in advance of a semester to ask.

facts.text: One centre's industrial workstations are described as loaded with named CAD and CAE packages, so laboratory software is procured and installed by somebody.

items.question: What will my assignment or thesis be checked against?
items.unanswered: No similarity-checking tool is named anywhere, so neither a student nor a supervisor can tell what a submission is compared with, what score matters, or whether a draft may be checked before it is submitted. The university states its expectations about plagiarism repeatedly and names no instrument for them.

items.question: I need to print, copy or scan something
answer: The library runs a reprography service and charges for it. Nothing else is published: no student printing, no print quota, no departmental printers, and no way to send a document to one.
Printing is among the highest-volume questions any university computing service gets, so its absence here is a gap rather than a sign that nothing exists.

facts.text: The Knowledge Resource Centre lists a reprography facility available on a payment basis.

items.question: Where should I keep my work, and is any of it backed up?
items.unanswered: No storage service, quota, shared drive or backup is described. A research group with data on a laboratory machine has nothing published telling it whether that data survives the machine.

items.question: I have deleted something important. Can it be recovered?
items.unanswered: Not published, and it cannot be answered until the previous question is. There is no stated retention period and no restore request route.

topics.title: Your own laptop, and the rooms you teach in
topics.summary: The machine you are required to own, and the equipment you are not.

items.question: What device do I need, and what happens if it fails in an examination?
answer: You sit examinations on your own device, so this is not an optional purchase. The university publishes what the device has to do rather than what to buy: a working camera and microphone, a supported operating system, a charge that outlasts the paper, a data connection as a fallback, and a power bank.
It says wireless is provided for digital examinations, and that queries during one go to the technical support centre or the online proctor.
No minimum specification, no recommended model, no loan scheme and no hardship provision is published. A student who cannot afford a suitable device has nowhere on this site to turn.

facts.text: Examinations are conducted digitally under a Bring Your Own Device policy; the device must be compatible in camera, microphone, operating system and other specifications informed from time to time, fully charged, with charging life beyond the maximum examination duration, a data pack in case of emergency and a power backup device.
The university states that it provides Wi-Fi connectivity for digital examinations and that the student may avail the network facilities of the university.

links.label: How examinations are taken

items.question: Something has gone wrong during a digital examination
answer: Ring the examination helpdesk. It is the one support service on the university's site that publishes a telephone number, an email address, a room and its opening hours together, and the university's own instruction is that login problems during an examination go to those numbers and nowhere else.
A device that will not start, a camera that will not work or a connection that drops during a paper is an examination problem before it is a computing one.

facts.text: Question papers are issued to the student's own device in a proctored environment and no hard copy is printed, so a failed device is a failed examination rather than an inconvenience.

items.question: My laptop is broken. Can the university repair it or lend me one?
items.unanswered: No repair service, loan pool or hardship scheme is published. Given that every examination is taken on a personally owned machine, whether one exists is a question with consequences for a student's degree rather than only for their convenience.

items.question: The projector in my teaching room will not work and my class has started
items.unanswered: No number to ring and nobody named, for 350-plus rooms fitted with smartboards and projectors. This is the shortest-fuse request on the whole page: an answer that takes a day is no answer at all.

facts.text: The university describes more than 350 hi-tech classrooms equipped with smartboards and LCD projectors, and multiple auditoriums with audio-visual facilities.

items.question: I teach here and I need the learning management system
items.unanswered: A learning management system is referred to once, in passing, in the biography of a member of the university's leadership. It is never named, never located, and there is no route to support for it.

facts.text: The only reference to a learning management system anywhere on the university's site is a leadership biography noting a role in implementing the university ERP and learning management systems.

topics.title: Security, and buying computing equipment
topics.summary: Suspicious messages, blocked access, and what to buy.

items.question: I have had a message asking for my password. Is it genuine?
items.unanswered: No statement of what the university will and will not ask you for, and no address to forward a suspicious message to. That single sentence — "we will never ask you for your password" — is the cheapest security control an institution owns, and it is not written down here.

facts.text: A handbook titled "Basics of Cyber Hygiene" is published in the university's student information index, which is the only security guidance on the site.

links.label: Student information, where the cyber hygiene handbook is published

items.question: I think my account has been compromised
items.unanswered: No incident reporting route, no out-of-hours contact and no procedure. Somebody has to decide who is told, how quickly, and what they do first.

items.question: My access to a journal database has stopped working
answer: It may have been blocked deliberately. The library prohibits systematic downloading from its subscribed databases, and states that breaking that rule leads to penal action and a block on the entire community of users — so one person's script takes the journals away from everybody.
If you are off campus, it is more likely the previous question: the subscriptions are licensed by network address and simply do not work from home.

facts.text: The Knowledge Resource Centre states that systematic downloading is strictly prohibited and will result in penal action and a block on the entire community of users.

items.question: I want to buy a computer for my department. What should I buy, and from whom?
items.unanswered: No standard specification, no approved supplier and no purchase route is published. A Purchase Committee exists and its membership is published; the process it runs is not.

links.label: Student information, where the Purchase Committee is listed

provenance: Each fact here was read from one of these published pages on the day the site was captured. They are the university's pages, not this one: when one of them changes, this page is wrong until it is rebuilt.

gapsIntroduction: The facts a person has to supply before this portal is worth publishing.

Until they are supplied, a missing value is shown as missing. A plausible wrong extension number sends somebody with a broken laptop to a stranger's desk, and a plausible wrong software entitlement has somebody install unlicensed software on the university's word. Both are worse than an admitted gap.

faculty.title: Faculty attached to the Centre
paragraphs: Distinct from the team answerable for running the services, because they are different things: a team keeps a service working, and a member of faculty is attached to the Centre. One person today.

Every fact below is read from the record this site already publishes about the person, and their profile is linked rather than restated. No role, title or office is asserted here, because none has been stated: “attached to the Centre” is the whole of the relationship, and a page that promoted it to a directorship would be inventing one.

pages.title: Reaching university systems from off campus
pages.lede: A virtual private network puts the machine in front of you on the university's network, wherever that machine is — so the things that only work on campus work from home. The university is introducing one. It has published nothing about it, and this page says so rather than inventing it.
pages.description: What a university VPN is for, who it is for, and the shape of connecting to one — with every value marked as a placeholder, because MIT-WPU has published nothing about the service yet.

notice.title: This service is not running yet, and every command below is a sample
paragraphs: There is no published gateway address, no client to install, no account to enable and nobody to ask. What is here is the shape of the thing, so that a reader knows what they will be doing and what they will need when it arrives.

Every value in every command is a placeholder written in capitals inside angle brackets. None of them will connect to anything, and none should be tried. When the service is announced, this page is replaced by its instructions and the marks come off.

sections.title: What a VPN does, and what it does not
paragraphs: It is a tunnel, not a permission. Your traffic goes to the university first and out from there, so a system that decides who you are by where you are coming from sees you as being on campus. That is the whole of the trick, and everything a VPN is good for follows from it.

What it is not is a way in for other people, a private network of your own, or anything to do with anonymity. It does not make a laptop safe, it does not encrypt what you do after the traffic leaves the university, and it is not a substitute for having an account on the thing you are trying to reach.

items.label: What it gives you
items.value: An address on the university's network, so services that check the address let you in.

items.label: What it does not give you
items.value: Access to anything you did not already have an account for. A tunnel is not an authorisation.

items.label: What it costs
items.value: Speed. Everything you do goes to Pune and back, including the things that did not need to.

items.label: Who it is likely to be for
items.value: not yet published here

sections.title: The things that only work on campus
paragraphs: One of them is published and is the reason this page exists at all: the library's subscriptions are licensed by network address, so a database that opens in the reading room refuses you at home. Everything else on this list is a guess about a university and not a statement about this one — which is exactly what a VPN page has to stop being.

facts.text: The Knowledge Resource Centre states that its online IP-based e-resources allow access anywhere on campus, and that its subscribed databases are accessible within the university premises.

links.label: Knowledge Resource Centre, including the free national collections that work from anywhere

sections.title: Getting access
paragraphs: Nothing here is a process the university has published. It is the shape such a process takes, set out so that whoever writes the real one has a list to work against and so that a reader knows what they will be asked for.

procedures.title: Ask for VPN access
procedures.summary: At the end of this you have an account enabled for the VPN and the details needed to configure a client.
procedures.applies_to: Nobody yet. There is no route to make this request.
before: A working university sign-in. If yours does not work, that is a different problem and it is on the Centre's own page.
A reason: which system you need to reach from off campus. Access to a network is normally granted for a purpose rather than in general.

steps.title: Check whether you need it at all
paragraphs: Most things a university publishes are on the open web and do not need a tunnel. It is worth two minutes: a VPN slows everything you do, and a request nobody needed to make is the most expensive kind.

steps.title: Make the request through whatever route the Centre publishes
paragraphs: No such route is published. When one is, it belongs here, and it is the second item on this page's work list.
steps.note: Do not send a password, a key, or a photograph of a screen to anybody as part of a request. No legitimate request for network access needs any of them.

steps.title: Receive the details
paragraphs: What arrives is an address to connect to, a name to connect as, and whichever second factor the university decides on. It is not a password sent in a message; a service that emails you a password is a service to raise a ticket about.

steps.title: Install the client the university names
paragraphs: Take it from the address the Centre gives you and from nowhere else. VPN clients are among the most impersonated software there is, and the copy at the top of a search result is not the one you want.
steps.note: Which client this will be is not published. Until it is, treat any page claiming to be MIT-WPU's VPN download as a phishing page, because today that is all it could be.

procedures.after: You are on when a system that refused you a minute ago lets you in.

sections.title: Connecting, once there is something to connect to
paragraphs: Two shapes, because universities publish two. Either the client is an application with a window, in which case there is nothing to type; or the tunnel is a command, in which case it is one line and can be scripted. Both are shown so that neither is a surprise.

commands.caption: Bring the tunnel up from a terminal

lines.comment: The address and the account name both arrive with your access; neither is published.

output: Connected. Your address on the university network is <ADDRESS-ASSIGNED-TO-YOU>.
commands.note: sudo is asking for the password of the machine in front of you, not for a university one. If something asks for your university password at this point, stop.

commands.caption: Check that it worked, before assuming it did

lines.comment: What the outside world now thinks your address is.
Whether the thing you actually wanted is now reachable.

commands.note: A tunnel that is up and a service that is reachable are two different questions, and answering only the first is how an afternoon goes.

commands.caption: Take it down when you have finished

lines.comment: Leaving it up sends everything you do through the university, including the things that are nobody's business there.

sections.title: What you are agreeing to when you connect
paragraphs: A VPN puts a machine the university does not own on to the network it is answerable for, so the terms matter more than they do for wireless in a corridor. None of these terms is published, and all five will have to be.

Two of them are worth stating now because they are true of every such service and cost somebody their access every year: the account is yours and is not lent, and the machine you connect from is your responsibility while it is on the network.

questionsIntroduction: Every one of them is unanswered, and each is a decision rather than a detail. They are kept here, in the reader's words, because a well-chosen question is a specification for whoever answers it.

topics.title: What has to be decided before this page is worth reading
topics.summary: Six decisions, in the order they block each other.

items.question: Who will be allowed to use the VPN?
items.unanswered: Whether it is for staff only, for research students, for all students, or granted per request. This is the first decision and every other one follows it: a service for four hundred staff and a service for thirty thousand students are not the same service.

items.question: What will the VPN let me reach that I cannot reach now?
items.unanswered: The list of systems that check the network address. The library's subscriptions are the only one the university has published; whether the learning management system, the examination systems, departmental servers or anything else are on it is unknown.

items.question: Will it get me into the library's databases from home?
items.unanswered: It is the obvious use and it is not stated. Some universities solve this with a VPN and some with a proxy that needs no client at all; the two are different work, and a reader cannot tell which is coming.

facts.text: The library states that its subscribed databases are accessible within the university premises, which is the constraint a VPN would lift.

items.question: Which client will I install, and where do I get it?
items.unanswered: Nothing is named. Until something is, there is no legitimate MIT-WPU VPN download anywhere, and anything claiming to be one is worth reporting rather than installing.

items.question: Will I need a second factor, and what will it be?
items.unanswered: A VPN account that needs only a password is a password away from being somebody else's. Whether a second factor is required, and whether it is an application, a message or a token, is not stated.

items.question: Is there anything I can do today instead?
answer: For the library, yes, partly. It lists freely available national collections that work from anywhere, and those need no tunnel and no sign-in.
For everything else, no. There is no published remote access of any kind — no VPN, no proxy, no off-campus sign-in — and there is nothing to configure while that remains true.

facts.text: The Knowledge Resource Centre lists free national collections alongside its subscribed databases.

links.label: Knowledge Resource Centre

pages.title: Remote access to C-DAC
pages.lede: Research computing beyond what a laboratory machine can do, on systems the university does not own and reaches over the network. The arrangement is being made; the account, the address and the terms are not settled, so what follows is the shape of the work rather than the instructions for it.
pages.description: How remote access to a national computing facility works in outline — accounts, keys, connecting, moving data and submitting work — with every hostname, account name and path marked as a placeholder, because MIT-WPU has published no arrangement and this page states none.

notice.title: Every instruction on this page is a sample
paragraphs: The university has published no arrangement with C-DAC, and this page describes none. What is here is the shape remote access to a national computing facility takes as such services are generally documented: you are given an account, you register a public key, you connect over SSH, you move your data, and you submit work to a scheduler rather than running it on the machine you logged in to.

Every hostname, account name, path, queue and project code below is a placeholder written in CAPITALS inside angle brackets. None of them is real, none of them will resolve, and none should be tried. The real values arrive with the account, from whoever issues it — not from this page, and not from a colleague's recollection.
When the arrangement is settled this page is replaced by its instructions. Until then, the list at the foot of the page is what has to be decided, and it is the useful part.

sections.title: When you need a machine you cannot walk up to
paragraphs: The threshold is not cleverness, it is arithmetic. Work belongs on a shared facility when it will not fit in the memory of a workstation, when it would take longer than you are prepared to leave a laptop running, or when it is the same calculation a few thousand times over with a different parameter each time. Everything below that threshold is faster on the machine you already have, because there is no queue in front of it.

What a facility of this kind gives you is not one large computer. It is a login machine you type on, a much larger set of compute machines you never log in to, a filesystem both can see, and a scheduler that decides when your work runs on the second set. Almost every mistake a first-time user makes comes from not yet believing the second sentence.

items.label: The login node
items.value: Where you land. For editing, moving files and submitting work — never for the work itself. It is shared by everyone logged in at that moment.

items.label: The compute nodes
items.value: Where the work actually runs, reached only through the scheduler. You do not choose one and you do not connect to it.

items.label: The scheduler
items.value: The queue. You describe what your job needs, it decides when that becomes available, and your job runs unattended when it does.

items.label: The allocation
items.value: The budget of machine time a project is granted. Work is charged against it, so a job that asks for eight times what it needs costs eight times as much.

items.label: Which facility, and which system
items.value: not yet settled

items.label: How an allocation is applied for
items.value: not yet settled

sections.title: What you will need before you apply
paragraphs: Three of these are yours to get ready now, and they are the reason this page is worth reading before there is anything to connect to. A key pair takes two minutes and is the thing most often missing when an account is issued.

items.label: An SSH key pair
items.value: Generated on the machine you will connect from. National facilities do not issue passwords for this, and the public half is what you send when you apply.

items.label: A working knowledge of the shell
items.value: You will be typing at a prompt with no windows on the far end. The introduction on this portal is enough to start with.

items.label: A project, and somebody answerable for it
items.value: Time on a national facility is granted to a piece of research rather than to a person, and normally needs a faculty member's name against it.

items.label: Data you may lawfully move
items.value: Anything with a person in it, anything under a licence that fixes where it may be held, and anything a collaborator gave you under terms — check before it leaves this university, not after.

sections.title: Getting an account
paragraphs: In outline, and marked as such throughout. No step below has a route, an address or a form behind it yet.

procedures.title: Apply for an account on a national facility
procedures.summary: At the end of this you have a username, a system to connect to, and a project your work is charged against.
procedures.applies_to: Nobody yet. This is the shape of the process, not the process.
before: A public key you generated yourself, and a private half you have never sent to anyone.
A one-paragraph description of the work and roughly what it will need.
The name of the faculty member answerable for the project.

steps.title: Generate a key pair if you have none
paragraphs: This part is real and you can do it today: the command is the same everywhere and does not depend on any arrangement being settled.

commands.caption: Generate a key pair

lines.comment: One key per person. The comment is only a label, so that you can tell your keys apart later.

commands.note: Give it a passphrase. A private key with no passphrase is a password written on a note that also fits in a backup.

steps.title: Send the public half with the application
paragraphs: The file ending in .pub, and nothing else. The other file is the private half and is never sent to anybody, including the people running the facility.

commands.caption: Read the public half so you can paste it
commands.note: One line, beginning ssh-ed25519 or ssh-rsa. If what you are looking at begins with five dashes and the word BEGIN, you have opened the private half; close it.

steps.note: This site will never publish a key, yours or anyone's, and neither should any page you are asked to paste one into.

steps.title: Wait for the account, and read what arrives
paragraphs: What comes back is a username, the address of a login node, the name of your project, and the facility's own conditions of use. Those conditions are the ones that bind you; nothing on this page overrides them.

steps.title: Connect once, immediately
paragraphs: Not because there is anything to do, but because an account that does not work is easiest to fix on the day it was issued and hardest three months later when the person who issued it has moved on.

sections.title: Connecting
paragraphs: One command the first time, and one word afterwards. The second is worth setting up on the first day: an address you type twenty times a week is an address you eventually mistype into somebody else's machine.

output: The authenticity of host '<LOGIN-NODE-YOU-WERE-GIVEN>' can't be established.
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)?
commands.note: Compare that fingerprint against the one the facility published before you answer yes. It is the only moment at which you can tell the real host from something standing in front of it, and it is the moment everybody skips.

commands.caption: Make it one word, in ~/.ssh/config on your own machine

lines.comment: Then, from anywhere:

commands.note: This file is read by ssh, scp and rsync alike, so the short name works for all three.

sections.title: Moving data in and out
paragraphs: Two tools, and the second one is the one to learn. `scp` copies a file; `rsync` copies what is different, resumes when it is interrupted and can be run again safely — which matters when the thing being moved is two hundred gigabytes over a network somebody else is also using.
Before any of it: check what you are allowed to move. A shared national facility is not a place to discover that a dataset had terms on it.

commands.caption: Copy one file up
Copy a directory up, resumably

lines.comment: -a keeps permissions and timestamps, -v says what it is doing, --partial keeps what it managed before the connection dropped.

commands.note: The trailing slash on the source is not decoration: without it rsync copies the directory INTO the target rather than copying its contents.

commands.caption: Bring results back

lines.comment: Same command, the arguments the other way round.

commands.note: Bring results back as you go rather than at the end. Scratch filesystems on shared facilities are routinely cleared, and the notice period is not always long.

sections.title: Running work: the scheduler
paragraphs: You do not run your calculation on the machine you logged in to. That machine is shared by everyone currently connected, and a job started on it slows all of them down and is usually killed. You write down what the work needs, hand that to the scheduler, and it runs when the machines are free.

Which scheduler this will be is not settled, and the commands differ between them. What does not differ is the four questions every one of them asks, and the answers are yours to work out before you can submit anything at all.

items.label: How many processors?
items.value: Asking for more than your program can use wastes the allocation and makes the wait longer, not shorter.

items.label: For how long?
items.value: An honest estimate plus a margin. Too short and the job is killed mid-run; too long and it queues behind everything.

items.label: How much memory?
items.value: The commonest cause of a job dying at three in the morning with nothing useful written down.

items.label: Which queue, and against which project?
items.value: Facilities separate short test runs from long ones, and charge the time to a project rather than to you.

items.label: Which scheduler the facility runs
items.value: not yet settled

items.label: What an allocation is worth, and how it is renewed
items.value: not yet settled

procedures.title: Submit a job
procedures.summary: The same four moves on every facility, whatever the scheduler is called.
procedures.applies_to: Sample only — the directives and commands below are placeholders, and the real ones come with the account.

steps.title: Write a submission script
paragraphs: A shell script with the scheduler's requests at the top and your work at the bottom. It is a file rather than a command line so that the run is reproducible and so that you can read, six months later, what you actually asked for.

commands.caption: A submission script, in outline

lines.comment: Every line beginning with the scheduler's directive marker is a request, not a comment.
Load what your program needs. Never assume it is there by default.
And then the work itself.

commands.note: Write the output file name with the job number in it. Two runs that overwrite each other's output is a morning gone.

steps.title: Submit it, and note the number

commands.caption: Hand the script to the scheduler
commands.note: That number is how you refer to the run from now on — to check it, to cancel it, and to ask anybody about it.

steps.title: Check on it without watching it
paragraphs: A queued job is not a broken one. Waiting is what a shared facility does, and a large request waits longer than a small one — which is an argument for asking for what you need rather than for what you would like.

commands.caption: See where your work is in the queue
Stop a run you no longer want

lines.comment: Do this as soon as you know. A job you have stopped caring about is still spending the project's allocation.

steps.title: Read the output, then bring it home
paragraphs: The output file the scheduler wrote is the first place to look when something went wrong, and it is usually the only place. Copy results back to storage you control rather than leaving them on a scratch filesystem.
steps.note: Test on a small input first, every time. A twelve-hour job that fails in its last minute because of a path typed wrongly is the standard first experience of a shared facility, and it is entirely avoidable.

procedures.after: The run is done when the output file stops growing and the job is no longer in the queue.

sections.title: What must not go on to a facility the university does not own
paragraphs: A shared national system is a third party, and moving data to it is a disclosure whatever the intention. Four categories, and the first one is the one that gets people into real trouble.

This page carries no credential of any kind, and neither will its replacement: not a key, not a password, not a project code that acts as one. A page behind a sign-in is still a web page, and it gets bookmarked, screenshotted and pasted into wikis.

items.label: Anything with a person in it
items.value: Student records, patient data, survey responses that can be traced back, photographs of identifiable people. Ask before, not after.

items.label: Data whose licence fixes where it may be held
items.value: Common in collaborations and in purchased datasets, and rarely remembered at the moment of copying.

items.label: Software you are not licensed to run there
items.value: A licence for a machine in a laboratory here does not travel to a machine somewhere else.

items.label: Any secret at all
items.value: A key, a token or a password in a script is a secret on a shared filesystem that other people's jobs run beside.

pages.title: Linux and SSH: enough to get started
pages.lede: A short working introduction for people whose research is about to need a machine they cannot walk up to. Not a course — the twenty-odd commands that account for most of a first week, in the order you meet them.
pages.description: A practical introduction to the Linux shell, files and permissions, SSH keys, the SSH configuration file, copying files with scp and rsync, keeping work alive with tmux, and what a job scheduler is for.

notice.title: The commands here are real; the addresses in them are not
paragraphs: Everything on this page works on any Linux or macOS machine, including the one in front of you, and it is worth trying there first. Where a command needs a host or an account, that part is a placeholder in capitals inside angle brackets and the block is marked as a sample — because this university has no host to name yet.
Nothing here is specific to MIT-WPU, and that is deliberate: what you learn on your own laptop is what you will type on somebody else's supercomputer.

sections.title: The shell, and where you are
paragraphs: A shell is a program that waits for you to type the name of another program. That is all it is. The prompt tells you which machine you are on and which directory you are in, and the single most common cause of a confusing afternoon is being wrong about one of those two.
Six commands account for most of what anyone does. Learn these and the rest can be looked up.

commands.caption: Where am I, and what is here

lines.comment: Print working directory: the folder you are in, as a full path.
List what is in it. -l for one per line with detail, -a to include the hidden dot-files.
Change directory. A bare cd goes home; cd .. goes up one.

commands.caption: Making, copying, moving, removing

lines.comment: Copy. -r to copy a whole directory.
Move — which is also how you rename.
Remove. There is no undo and there is no wastebasket.

commands.note: rm -rf is the command that ends careers. It deletes a directory and everything under it without asking, and a stray space in the wrong place makes the argument something much larger than you meant. Read the line before pressing return, every time.

commands.caption: When you do not know what a command does

lines.comment: The manual is on the machine and does not need a network.
Most modern commands answer this too.

commands.note: Press q to leave the manual. Not knowing that is the reason most people leave it by closing the window.

sections.title: Files, and who may do what to them
paragraphs: Every file carries three permissions — read, write, execute — for three audiences: you, your group, everybody else. `ls -l` shows them as nine characters. This is worth ten minutes now, because SSH refuses to use a private key whose permissions are wrong and the error message does not say so plainly.

The numbers are the same three permissions written as bits: 4 read, 2 write, 1 execute, added together per audience. So 600 is "I may read and write it, nobody else may do anything", and 755 is "I may do anything, everybody else may read and run it".

items.value: Yours alone, read and write. What a private key must be.
Yours to edit, everyone else's to read. The default for an ordinary file.
Yours alone, including entering it. What ~/.ssh must be.
Yours to change, everyone else's to enter or run. The default for a directory or a script.

commands.caption: Read the permissions, then set them

lines.comment: The first ten characters of each line are the type and the nine permissions.
The two that SSH insists on.
A script you want to be able to run by name.

commands.note: "Permissions 0644 for 'id_ed25519' are too open" is SSH refusing to use a key anybody on the machine could read. chmod 600 is the whole fix.

sections.title: SSH keys: what they are and how to make one
paragraphs: A key pair is two files. The public half is not a secret and is what you hand out; the private half is the secret and never leaves the machine it was made on. A remote system that has your public half can check that you hold the private half without ever seeing it, which is why this is better than a password and why no shared facility issues passwords for it.
One key per person, not one per machine you connect to. If you work from a laptop and a desktop, that is two keys, and both public halves get registered.

procedures.title: Make a key pair
procedures.summary: Two minutes, once, on each machine you will connect from.
procedures.applies_to: macOS and Linux, and Windows 10 or later in PowerShell or WSL.

steps.title: Check whether you already have one

commands.caption: List the keys on this machine
commands.note: A file ending in .pub means you have a key. Use it. Making a second one does not add security and does add a thing to keep track of.

steps.title: Generate the pair

commands.caption: Generate an ed25519 key pair

lines.comment: ed25519 rather than RSA: shorter, faster, and the current default everywhere.

output: Enter file in which to save the key (~/.ssh/id_ed25519):

steps.note: Give it a passphrase. It is asked for once per session rather than once per connection, and it is the only thing standing between a stolen laptop and everywhere that laptop could reach.

lines.comment: What the agent currently holds.

sections.title: Connecting, and the fingerprint nobody checks
paragraphs: The first connection to any machine asks you to confirm its fingerprint. That prompt is the only moment at which you can tell the machine you meant from something standing in front of it, and it is the moment everyone clicks through. Compare it with what the service published, once, and the machine is remembered afterwards.

commands.caption: Open a session
output: The authenticity of host '<HOST-YOU-WERE-GIVEN>' can't be established.
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])?
commands.note: Type exit, or press Ctrl-D, to come back.

commands.caption: When it will not connect, ask it why

lines.comment: -v once for a little, -vvv for more than you want.

commands.note: The useful lines are the ones naming which key was offered and what the server said about it. "Permission denied (publickey)" almost always means the public half was never registered, or the private half is not the one being offered.

sections.title: Making it one word
paragraphs: `~/.ssh/config` on your own machine turns an address you would otherwise retype into a short name. It is read by ssh, scp and rsync alike, so setting it up once fixes all three, and it is the single highest-value ten minutes on this page.

commands.caption: A host entry in ~/.ssh/config

lines.comment: Indentation is conventional rather than required; keep it anyway.
Keeps a session from being dropped while you think.

commands.caption: And then, from anywhere
commands.note: The config file itself should be readable only by you: chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config.

sections.title: Moving files between machines
paragraphs: `scp` for one file, `rsync` for everything else. rsync copies only what differs, resumes an interrupted transfer and can be run again safely — which is what you want the moment the thing being copied is larger than a coffee break.

commands.caption: One file, up and then back
commands.note: The lone dot means "into the directory I am in now".

commands.caption: A directory, resumably

lines.comment: -a preserves permissions and times, -v narrates, --partial keeps what arrived before a drop.
Show what WOULD be copied and copy nothing. Worth doing first, every time.

commands.note: The trailing slash on the source is not decoration. With it, the contents are copied; without it, the directory itself is copied inside the target, which is how people end up with results/results/results.

sections.title: Keeping work alive when your connection drops
paragraphs: Close a terminal and everything running in it dies with it, which on a train is a two-hour job lost at ninety minutes. `tmux` puts the session on the far end of the connection rather than in your terminal, so it survives the connection going away and is still there when you come back.
Three commands is the whole of what most people need.

commands.caption: Start, leave, and come back

lines.comment: Start a named session. Name it after the work, not after the day.
Detach: press Ctrl-b, let go, then press d. The session keeps running.
What is still running.
Reattach, from the same machine or a different one.

commands.note: Ctrl-b is tmux's attention key: every tmux command is Ctrl-b followed by something. Ctrl-b then c makes a new window inside the session, Ctrl-b then n moves to the next one.

sections.title: Why you do not run your work on the machine you logged in to
paragraphs: On a shared research system the machine you land on is a doorway, not a workshop. It is shared with everyone else currently connected, and a calculation started there slows all of them down; most facilities kill such processes automatically, and some suspend the account.

Instead you describe the work in a small script and hand it to a scheduler, which runs it unattended on machines you never log in to. There are several schedulers and their commands differ, but all of them ask the same four questions, and having the answers is what makes the difference between a first day that works and one that does not.

items.label: How many processors?
items.value: More than your program can actually use makes the wait longer and the bill bigger, not the run faster.

items.label: For how long?
items.value: Your honest estimate plus a margin. Under-ask and it is killed part-way; over-ask and it queues behind everything else.

items.label: How much memory?
items.value: The commonest reason a long job dies overnight leaving nothing useful behind.

items.label: Charged to what?
items.value: Time is granted to a project rather than to a person, so a submission normally names one.

sections.title: What this page deliberately does not cover
paragraphs: It is a first week, not a course. Shell scripting beyond a straight run of commands, package and environment management, version control, containers, parallel programming and performance measurement are each larger than everything above put together, and a page that gestured at them would teach nobody anything.

The university publishes no training in any of it, and no reading list. That is on the work list below rather than filled in here with somebody's favourite links: a recommendation is an institutional statement, and this page does not make those on the university's behalf.

pages.title: Software: what you may install, and how to get it
pages.lede: Three questions account for almost all of this: is it free to me, do I have to buy it, and where do I get it. The university has answered none of them, and this page shows the shape of the answer with every cell marked as missing rather than guessed.

notice.title: No entitlement in the table below has been published
paragraphs: Every cell reading "Not yet published" is work for a person, not a statement that the software is unavailable. Until somebody fills them in, buy nothing on the strength of this table and install nothing on the strength of a colleague's recollection: telling somebody they may install a product the university does not license puts both them and the university in the wrong.

Whatever is decided, no licence key, serial or activation code will appear on this page or on any page of this site. A page behind a sign-in is still a web page, and it gets bookmarked, screenshotted and pasted into wikis. The build refuses to publish one.

sections.title: How to read the table
paragraphs: It is arranged by entitlement rather than as a catalogue of products, because a list of things that exist somewhere in the university answers none of the three questions. Each row is a product people ask about; each column is one of the four things you need to know before installing it.

The fourth column is the one institutions forget and are then audited on. A licence that follows a person who has left, or a machine that keeps a departmental key after it is sold, is how a compliant institution stops being one.

What to include when there is somewhere to send it: the product and version, what you need it for, how many people, and whether a grant will pay. Half of a licensing decision is arithmetic, and a request without those four numbers turns into three messages.

paragraphs: The same six, in the same order, on every page — so a reader who has used one manual can use all of them without learning a second layout, and so that what is missing from one is comparable with what is missing from another.

Most of these services are documented nowhere at all. A manual that is three honest sentences and a list of six unanswered questions is more use than one padded out with what a service of that kind usually does: the padding reads as fact, and the reader acts on it.

tasksIntroduction: As on Android, from the register's own description.

What is known about the Computing Resources Centre

manuals.lede: Where employment is administered: leave, attendance, payroll and the personal record behind them. The intranet's Human Resources page is the fuller account; this is the manual for the application itself.
purpose: Everything about being employed here that is a transaction rather than a conversation. Applying for leave, seeing what leave remains, and whatever the university has configured it to hold about pay.

What it actually shows, and when, is not published — which matters more here than on most of these services, because an employee planning a year around a leave balance needs to know whether the number they are looking at is current.
problemsIntroduction: There is nothing to point at. The register gives a launch address and an empty support route, so when the sign-in fails or a leave balance is wrong there is no published route to anybody who can look at it.
ownerIntroduction: The Human Resources Office publishes an email address and nothing else. The system itself is the Centre's; the records in it are the Office's, and which of the two a given problem belongs to is not stated anywhere.

links.label: Pay, leave and your appointment
links.note: The fuller account, including what HROne is and is not the answer to

manuals.lede: An employee identity card in digital form, and a visiting card with it. A name in the register, an address, and nothing else written down anywhere.
manuals.completenessNote: Five of the six are unanswered. This manual exists because the service does, and because a service in the register with no page is an omission nobody notices; what it mostly records is how little is known.
ownerIntroduction: The Human Resources Office holds employee identity, so the record is theirs; whether the application is theirs or the Centre's is not stated.

manuals.lede: Booking a court, a pitch or a session. The register says it is open to everyone with a university sign-in, which makes it the most widely available service on this list.
purpose: Reserving campus sports facilities and whatever recreation the university runs through the same system. It is one of only two services here the register opens to everybody with a sign-in rather than to a named audience.
ownerIntroduction: The Sports Department, which is one of the few teams on the intranet that publishes a telephone number, an email address and a request route.

links.label: Books, rooms and equipment, including how sports facilities are booked

manuals.lede: Booking a classroom, a laboratory or a hall. Open to everyone with a university sign-in, and the answer to a question the help pages currently cannot answer.
purpose: Reserving teaching and event space. It is worth naming plainly because the university's public pages do not: a reader looking for how to book a hall finds no route, and this is it.
problemsIntroduction: No support route is registered, and no owner is published for room booking anywhere on the university's pages — which is listed on the help page as one of the services nobody has been made answerable for.
ownerIntroduction: Unsettled. The application is in the computing register; the rooms belong to whoever timetables them, and no page names that office.

links.label: Books, rooms and equipment
links.note: Where room booking is currently listed as having no published owner
